# C# entities

If your game is written in C#, your own classes can be placeable entities without writing a `.tres` definition. The addon reads your source files, finds classes marked as entities, and treats their signals as outputs, their exported members as keys and their marked methods as inputs. The editor lists them in the Entities panel next to the built in library.

## Add the helper once

The attributes live in a small helper file that is not shipped with the addon. In the editor, open the Reference panel (*View > Panels > Reference*) and press **Add C# helper to project**. It writes `res://addons/func_godot/csharp/GodotTrench.cs`, which defines `[GodotTrenchEntity]`, `[GodotTrenchInput]` and a static `GodotTrench` class for I/O from C#. Without it, code using the attributes does not compile.

Running C# entities needs the .NET build of Godot. The scan that finds them is plain GDScript, so the editor sees them either way.

cards.code:
[GlobalClass]
[GodotTrenchEntity("npc_guard", Description = "Patrolling guard",
    Color = "#ff4040ff", Size = "-16 0 -16 16 64 16")]
public partial class NpcGuard : CharacterBody3D
{
    [Signal] public delegate void AlertedEventHandler(Node activator, int level); // output "alerted"
    [Export] public float WalkSpeed { get; set; } = 3.5f;                          // key "walk_speed"
    [GodotTrenchInput] public void Alert(Node activator) { }                        // input "alert"
}

cards.md:
Names are converted to the snake_case the map uses, and back again at runtime, so the map input `alert` calls `Alert` and the key `walk_speed` sets `WalkSpeed`. If no method in the class has `[GodotTrenchInput]`, every public `void` method with a capitalized name becomes an input instead. Marking even one method turns that off, which is usually what you want once a class grows helper methods.

`[GlobalClass]` is required, because the builder finds the class by name, and without it the entity builds as a plain node. `Size` is the bounding box as mins and maxs in map units, and `Solid = true` makes a brush entity, like a door, instead of a point entity.

Key values are assigned to your members automatically. If you would rather read them yourself, implement `_func_godot_apply_properties(Dictionary props)`; the helper has readers like `GodotTrench.Float(props, "walk_speed", 3.5f)` that handle the string parsing.

## Where the addon looks

There are two settings, because the editor and the build scan at different times. The game config export, which feeds the editor, scans the folders in the config resource's *Csharp Source Dirs*. The map build scans the folders in the project setting `godottrench/csharp_entity_dirs`. Both default to `res://` and skip `addons`, `.godot`, `bin`, `obj` and hidden folders. The plugin registers the project setting, so narrowing it is a matter of editing the list under *Project Settings > Godottrench*.

C# definitions are only consulted for classnames the FGD does not define, so a C# class cannot replace a library entity by using the same name.

## I/O from C#

Reacting to another entity's output is ordinary Godot signal code. To fire outputs or call inputs the way the map does, use the helper:

The Reference panel generates all of this for any class. Pick an entity and it shows how to use it from GDScript and C#, a class skeleton for writing a new one, and the FGD resource. The editor's MCP server offers the same text through its `code_reference` tool.
